title: Simulacro IIE 1: Net-Zero Industry Act / PERTE de Descarbonización Industrial

listening.title: Making clean technologies in Europe: the industrial challenge of the decade
listening.text:
For most of the past two decades, Europe has been remarkably good at inventing clean technologies and remarkably poor at manufacturing them at scale. European laboratories pioneered many of the advances behind modern solar cells, wind turbines and electrolysers, yet today the overwhelming majority of the solar modules installed on European rooftops are produced elsewhere, and the continent's share of global battery cell production remains modest. This imbalance is no longer seen as a mere commercial issue. It has become a question of economic security.

The Net-Zero Industry Act is the European Union's response. Its central ambition is that, by 2030, the Union should be able to manufacture at least forty per cent of the net-zero technologies it needs to deploy each year. The list of technologies covered is broad: solar photovoltaic and solar thermal equipment, onshore and offshore wind, batteries and energy storage, heat pumps, electrolysers and fuel cells, grid technologies, and carbon capture and storage, among others.

The Act does not, in itself, create a large new pot of money. Instead, it seeks to remove the obstacles that make Europe a slow and expensive place to build a factory. The first of these is permitting. Under the new rules, Member States must set up single points of contact, and permit-granting procedures for manufacturing projects are subject to binding time limits, which are shorter still for projects recognised as strategic. Too often, investors have waited longer for a permit than it takes to build the plant itself.

The second lever is demand. Public authorities spend a considerable share of the Union's wealth on goods and services every year, and renewable energy auctions shape the market for wind and solar equipment. The Act requires these procedures to take into account criteria other than price, such as sustainability, cybersecurity and resilience, in other words the risk of depending excessively on a single supplier. The aim is not to close the market, but to stop the lowest bid from being the only consideration.

A third element concerns skills. Industry associations warn that the shortage of qualified technicians, welders and engineers could prove as serious a bottleneck as access to finance. The Act therefore supports so-called Net-Zero Industry Academies, which are meant to train large numbers of workers within a few years, in partnership with companies and training providers.

Finally, the Act sets an objective that has received less public attention but matters greatly for heavy industry: an annual injection capacity of fifty million tonnes of carbon dioxide in geological storage sites by 2030, with oil and gas producers expected to contribute to this effort.

Critics point out that the United States and China are offering far more generous subsidies, and that simplifying procedures will not, on its own, offset higher energy prices in Europe. Supporters reply that predictability is itself a form of support, and that a clear regulatory framework can unlock private investment far larger than any public budget.

What is beyond dispute is the scale of the challenge. Building factories takes years, and the decisions taken in the next two or three will largely determine whether Europe's energy transition is powered by technologies made in Europe, or merely installed there.

keyPoints: Europe invents clean technologies but manufactures few of them (most solar modules imported, small share of battery cells); this is now an economic-security issue.

The Net-Zero Industry Act aims for the EU to manufacture at least 40% of the net-zero technologies it deploys each year by 2030, across a broad list (solar, wind, batteries, heat pumps, electrolysers, grids, CCS).
The Act does not create a big new fund; it removes obstacles to building factories in Europe.
Permitting: single points of contact and binding deadlines, even shorter for strategic projects.
Demand: public procurement and renewable auctions must weigh non-price criteria (sustainability, cybersecurity, resilience/supplier diversification) without closing the market.
Skills: Net-Zero Industry Academies to address shortages of technicians, welders and engineers.
CO2 storage target: 50 million tonnes of annual injection capacity by 2030, with a contribution from oil and gas producers.
Debate: critics cite bigger US/Chinese subsidies and high EU energy prices; supporters argue regulatory predictability attracts private investment.
The next two or three years will decide whether the transition uses technologies made in Europe or merely installed there.

Although European researchers pioneered many solar, wind and hydrogen technologies, most of the equipment installed in Europe, notably solar modules and battery cells, is produced abroad, a dependence now regarded as a matter of economic security.

The Net-Zero Industry Act sets the goal that, by 2030, the EU should produce at least 40% of the net-zero technologies it deploys annually, a category ranging from heat pumps and electrolysers to grid equipment and carbon capture. First, it speeds up permitting through single points of contact and binding deadlines, which are even shorter for strategic projects. While critics argue that these measures cannot match US and Chinese subsidies or offset high energy costs, supporters contend that regulatory certainty will mobilise private capital. In any case, the decisions taken in the coming years will prove decisive.

spanish.title: El Gobierno abre una nueva convocatoria de ayudas del PERTE de Descarbonización Industrial
spanish.text:
El Ministerio de Industria y Turismo ha publicado en el Boletín Oficial del Estado la orden por la que se establecen las bases reguladoras y se efectúa la convocatoria de una nueva línea de ayudas para la descarbonización de la industria manufacturera, en el marco del Proyecto Estratégico para la Recuperación y Transformación Económica (PERTE) de Descarbonización Industrial. La convocatoria, dotada con 500 millones de euros, se financiará con cargo a fondos europeos y a los Presupuestos Generales del Estado.

Las ayudas se destinan a proyectos que reduzcan de forma significativa las emisiones de gases de efecto invernadero de los procesos productivos, especialmente en los sectores intensivos en energía, como el siderúrgico, el cementero, el químico, el cerámico o el del vidrio. Serán subvencionables, entre otras, las actuaciones de electrificación de procesos térmicos, la sustitución de combustibles fósiles por hidrógeno renovable o biometano, la mejora de la eficiencia energética, la captura de carbono y la integración de fuentes renovables para autoconsumo.

Podrán ser beneficiarias las empresas de cualquier tamaño que desarrollen una actividad industrial en España, ya sea de manera individual o agrupadas. Para garantizar la participación del tejido productivo de menor dimensión, se reserva un porcentaje del presupuesto a las pequeñas y medianas empresas, que podrán además beneficiarse de intensidades de ayuda superiores, de conformidad con el marco europeo de ayudas de Estado.

Los proyectos deberán acreditar una reducción mínima de las emisiones directas del treinta por ciento respecto de la situación de partida, calculada conforme a la metodología que figura en el anexo de la orden. Asimismo, habrán de respetar el principio de no causar un perjuicio significativo al medio ambiente, conocido por sus siglas en inglés DNSH, y no podrán haberse iniciado antes de la presentación de la solicitud.

La tramitación se llevará a cabo en régimen de concurrencia competitiva. Las solicitudes se presentarán exclusivamente por vía electrónica a través de la sede electrónica del Ministerio, en el plazo de dos meses a contar desde el día siguiente al de la publicación del extracto de la convocatoria. La evaluación tendrá en cuenta, entre otros criterios, el volumen de emisiones evitadas por euro de ayuda, la madurez tecnológica del proyecto, su efecto tractor sobre la cadena de valor y la creación o el mantenimiento de empleo de calidad.

Los beneficiarios deberán ejecutar las actuaciones en un plazo máximo de veinticuatro meses desde la notificación de la resolución de concesión y justificar la ayuda mediante cuenta justificativa con informe de auditor. Se podrán conceder anticipos de hasta el cincuenta por ciento del importe concedido, previa constitución de las garantías correspondientes.

Según ha señalado el Ministerio, esta línea complementa las convocatorias anteriores del PERTE, que ya han movilizado inversiones privadas por un importe muy superior al de la ayuda pública concedida. La industria representa en torno a una quinta parte de las emisiones de gases de efecto invernadero en España, por lo que su descarbonización resulta imprescindible para alcanzar los objetivos del Plan Nacional Integrado de Energía y Clima (PNIEC) sin comprometer la competitividad ni el empleo.

El Ministerio celebrará próximamente una jornada informativa telemática dirigida a empresas, asociaciones sectoriales y consultoras, en la que se resolverán las dudas sobre los requisitos de la convocatoria y el procedimiento de solicitud.

modelTranslation:
Government launches a new call for aid under the Industrial Decarbonisation PERTE

The Ministry of Industry and Tourism has published in the Official State Gazette (BOE) the order laying down the regulatory bases and launching the call for a new aid scheme for the decarbonisation of manufacturing industry, within the framework of the Strategic Project for Economic Recovery and Transformation (PERTE) for Industrial Decarbonisation. The call, which has a budget of 500 million euros, will be financed from European funds and the General State Budget.

The aid is intended for projects that significantly reduce greenhouse gas emissions from production processes, particularly in energy-intensive sectors such as steel, cement, chemicals, ceramics and glass. Eligible measures include, among others, the electrification of thermal processes, the replacement of fossil fuels with renewable hydrogen or biomethane, improvements in energy efficiency, carbon capture and the integration of renewable sources for self-consumption.

Companies of any size carrying out an industrial activity in Spain will be eligible, either individually or as part of a consortium. To ensure the participation of smaller businesses, a share of the budget is reserved for small and medium-sized enterprises, which may also benefit from higher aid intensities, in accordance with the European State aid framework.

Projects must demonstrate a minimum reduction of thirty per cent in direct emissions compared with the baseline, calculated according to the methodology set out in the annex to the order. They must also comply with the principle of "do no significant harm" to the environment, known by its English acronym DNSH, and may not have started before the application is submitted.

Applications will be processed under a competitive procedure. They must be submitted exclusively online through the Ministry's electronic office within two months from the day following the publication of the summary of the call. The assessment will take into account, among other criteria, the volume of emissions avoided per euro of aid, the technological maturity of the project, its knock-on effect on the value chain and the creation or retention of quality jobs.

Beneficiaries must carry out the measures within a maximum of twenty-four months from notification of the award decision and must account for the aid by submitting an expenditure report accompanied by an auditor's report. Advance payments of up to fifty per cent of the amount awarded may be granted, subject to the provision of the corresponding guarantees.

According to the Ministry, this scheme complements previous PERTE calls, which have already mobilised private investment far exceeding the public aid granted. Industry accounts for around one fifth of greenhouse gas emissions in Spain, so its decarbonisation is essential to meet the targets of the National Integrated Energy and Climate Plan (NECP) without undermining competitiveness or employment.

The Ministry will shortly hold an online information session for companies, trade associations and consultancies, at which questions about the requirements of the call and the application procedure will be answered.

title: Simulacro IIE 2: CBAM, acero y cemento / Reglamento de productos de construcción

listening.title: Putting a price on carbon at the border
listening.text:
For almost twenty years, European steelmakers and cement producers have paid for the carbon dioxide they emit under the EU Emissions Trading System. Their competitors outside Europe, in most cases, have not. To prevent production simply moving abroad, a phenomenon economists call carbon leakage, the most exposed sectors have received a large part of their emission allowances free of charge. That arrangement protected jobs, but it also weakened the incentive to invest in cleaner processes.

The Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism, usually shortened to CBAM, is designed to resolve this dilemma. In essence, it asks importers of certain carbon-intensive goods to pay a price for the emissions embedded in those goods, equivalent to the price a European producer would have paid. The products covered in the first stage are iron and steel, cement, aluminium, fertilisers, hydrogen and electricity, sectors which together account for a significant share of industrial emissions.

The mechanism has been introduced gradually. During a transitional phase that began in October 2023, importers only had to report the emissions embedded in their goods, without paying anything. That period proved to be a steep learning curve. Many importers discovered that their suppliers simply did not measure emissions at installation level, and the Commission responded by simplifying the rules, notably by exempting small importers below an annual threshold of fifty tonnes, while still covering the vast majority of emissions.

From 2026, the definitive regime applies. Importers must be authorised as CBAM declarants and will have to surrender certificates corresponding to their embedded emissions, with a deduction for any carbon price already paid in the country of production. At the same time, the free allowances granted to European producers will be phased out progressively until the mid-2030s, so that domestic and foreign producers eventually face the same carbon cost.

Supporters argue that the mechanism is the logical complement to an ambitious climate policy. Without it, Europe would be exporting its emissions along with its industrial jobs. They also point to an encouraging side effect: several trading partners have begun to design or strengthen their own carbon pricing systems, partly to keep the revenue at home rather than paying it at the European border.

The concerns, however, are considerable. Exporters in developing countries fear that the reporting burden and the cost will shut them out of the European market. European manufacturers who use steel or aluminium as inputs, such as machinery or automotive firms, worry that their costs will rise while imported finished goods remain outside the scope of the mechanism. And European exporters will lose their free allowances without receiving equivalent protection on world markets.

For cement and steel, the stakes are particularly high. Both sectors depend on processes, such as the calcination of limestone or the reduction of iron ore with coke, that cannot be decarbonised merely by switching to renewable electricity. They will require hydrogen-based steelmaking, carbon capture and new low-clinker cements, all of which demand heavy investment. The border mechanism, its designers hope, will finally give those investments a fair chance of paying off.

keyPoints: EU steel and cement producers pay for CO2 under the ETS, but most foreign competitors do not; free allowances were used to prevent carbon leakage, at the cost of weaker incentives to invest.
CBAM makes importers pay a carbon price on embedded emissions equivalent to that paid by EU producers; first sectors: iron and steel, cement, aluminium, fertilisers, hydrogen and electricity.
Transitional phase from October 2023: reporting only; data proved hard to obtain, so rules were simplified (exemption for small importers below 50 tonnes a year while covering most emissions).
Definitive regime from 2026: authorised declarants surrender certificates, minus carbon prices already paid abroad; free allowances phased out until the mid-2030s.
Supporters: logical complement to climate policy, avoids exporting emissions and jobs, and encourages other countries to adopt carbon pricing.
Concerns: burden for exporters in developing countries; downstream EU manufacturers face higher input costs; EU exporters lose free allowances without protection abroad.
Steel and cement have process emissions (limestone calcination, coke-based reduction) that require hydrogen, CCS and low-clinker cements; CBAM should help those investments pay off.
modelSummary:
The text explains the purpose, design and controversies of the EU's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM). European heavy industry has long paid for its emissions under the Emissions Trading System, unlike most foreign rivals; to avoid carbon leakage, exposed sectors received free allowances, which, however, reduced the incentive to decarbonise.

CBAM requires importers of carbon-intensive goods, initially iron and steel, cement, aluminium, fertilisers, hydrogen and electricity, to pay for their embedded emissions at the same price as EU producers. After a transitional reporting phase starting in October 2023, which revealed serious data gaps and led to simplifications such as exempting importers of under 50 tonnes a year, the definitive regime began in 2026. Authorised declarants must now surrender certificates, minus any carbon price paid abroad, while free allowances are gradually withdrawn until the mid-2030s.

Advocates regard CBAM as the natural complement to ambitious climate policy and note that it is prompting other countries to introduce carbon pricing. Critics highlight the burden on developing-country exporters, higher input costs for downstream European manufacturers and the loss of free allocation for EU exporters.

Finally, the text stresses that steel and cement face process emissions that renewable electricity alone cannot eliminate, so costly technologies such as hydrogen-based steelmaking and carbon capture are needed; CBAM is meant to make them viable.

spanish.title: Nuevo marco europeo para los productos de construcción: obligaciones para fabricantes e importadores
spanish.text:
El nuevo Reglamento europeo de productos de construcción, que sustituye progresivamente a la normativa vigente desde 2011, introduce cambios sustanciales en las condiciones de comercialización de estos productos en el mercado interior. El Ministerio de Industria y Turismo, en colaboración con las comunidades autónomas, ha elaborado una nota informativa con el fin de orientar a fabricantes, importadores y distribuidores durante el período transitorio.

El Reglamento mantiene el marcado CE como elemento central del sistema. Este marcado indica que el producto es conforme con las prestaciones declaradas en relación con sus características esenciales, como la resistencia mecánica, la reacción al fuego o el aislamiento térmico, evaluadas de acuerdo con las especificaciones técnicas armonizadas. No obstante, la declaración de prestaciones se complementa ahora con una declaración de conformidad respecto de determinados requisitos aplicables al producto.

Una de las principales novedades es la incorporación de requisitos de sostenibilidad. Los fabricantes deberán informar, cuando así lo establezcan los actos delegados correspondientes, sobre el potencial de calentamiento global de sus productos a lo largo de su ciclo de vida, calculado con arreglo a una metodología común. Se pretende así que los proyectistas y las administraciones públicas puedan comparar productos de forma objetiva y que la contratación pública favorezca las soluciones con menor huella de carbono.

Asimismo, el Reglamento prevé la implantación de un pasaporte digital de producto, que permitirá acceder por medios electrónicos a la información técnica, a las instrucciones de uso y seguridad y a los datos necesarios para la reutilización, la reparación o el reciclado del producto al final de su vida útil. Las instrucciones y la información de seguridad podrán facilitarse en formato digital, si bien el usuario podrá seguir solicitando una copia en papel.

Las obligaciones de los operadores económicos se definen con mayor precisión. El importador deberá comprobar que el fabricante ha llevado a cabo la evaluación y verificación de la constancia de las prestaciones, que el producto va acompañado de la documentación exigida y que lleva el marcado CE. Los distribuidores y las plataformas de venta en línea quedan igualmente sujetos a deberes específicos de diligencia.

Por otra parte, se refuerzan los requisitos aplicables a los organismos notificados, que deberán demostrar su competencia técnica, imparcialidad e independencia, y se amplían las facultades de las autoridades de vigilancia del mercado para retirar del mercado los productos que no cumplan o que presenten un riesgo para la salud o la seguridad de las personas.

La aplicación del Reglamento será gradual. Durante el período transitorio, las normas armonizadas adoptadas con arreglo a la normativa anterior seguirán siendo de aplicación hasta que sean sustituidas por las nuevas especificaciones técnicas, de acuerdo con el calendario que establezca la Comisión Europea para cada familia de productos.

El Ministerio recuerda que el incumplimiento de estas obligaciones podrá dar lugar a la imposición de sanciones conforme a la legislación de seguridad industrial, y recomienda a las empresas del sector que revisen cuanto antes sus procedimientos de control de producción en fábrica.

modelTranslation:
New European framework for construction products: obligations for manufacturers and importers

The new European Construction Products Regulation, which is gradually replacing the legislation in force since 2011, introduces substantial changes to the conditions under which these products are placed on the internal market. The Ministry of Industry and Tourism, in cooperation with the autonomous communities, has drawn up an information note to guide manufacturers, importers and distributors during the transitional period.

The Regulation keeps CE marking at the heart of the system. This marking indicates that the product conforms to the performance declared in relation to its essential characteristics, such as mechanical strength, reaction to fire or thermal insulation, assessed in accordance with harmonised technical specifications. However, the declaration of performance is now supplemented by a declaration of conformity with certain requirements applicable to the product.

One of the main new features is the introduction of sustainability requirements. Where the relevant delegated acts so provide, manufacturers will have to report the global warming potential of their products throughout their life cycle, calculated according to a common methodology. The aim is to enable designers and public authorities to compare products objectively and to ensure that public procurement favours solutions with a lower carbon footprint.

The Regulation also provides for the introduction of a digital product passport, which will give electronic access to technical information, instructions for use and safety information, and the data needed to reuse, repair or recycle the product at the end of its service life. Instructions and safety information may be provided in digital format, although users will still be able to request a paper copy.

The obligations of economic operators are defined more precisely. Importers will have to check that the manufacturer has carried out the assessment and verification of constancy of performance, that the product is accompanied by the required documentation and that it bears the CE marking. Distributors and online marketplaces are likewise subject to specific due diligence obligations.

In addition, the requirements applicable to notified bodies are tightened, as they will have to demonstrate their technical competence, impartiality and independence, and the powers of market surveillance authorities are extended so that they can withdraw from the market any products that do not comply or that pose a risk to human health or safety.

The Regulation will be applied gradually. During the transitional period, harmonised standards adopted under the previous legislation will continue to apply until they are replaced by the new technical specifications, in line with the timetable to be set by the European Commission for each product family.

The Ministry points out that failure to comply with these obligations may result in penalties under industrial safety legislation, and recommends that companies in the sector review their factory production control procedures as soon as possible.

meta.topic: Artificial intelligence and cybersecurity in industrial control systems
meta.source: Generado para el proyecto (original), formato según memorias de los tribunales

title: Simulacro IIE 3: IA y ciberseguridad en sistemas de control industrial / Plan de ciberseguridad industrial

listening.title: When the factory floor goes online
listening.text:
Not so long ago, the computers that controlled a chemical plant, a water treatment works or an electricity substation lived in a world of their own. They ran specialised software, spoke obscure communication protocols and were physically separated from the internet. Engineers called this separation the air gap, and for decades it was considered sufficient protection.

That world has largely disappeared. To improve efficiency, operators have connected their industrial control systems to corporate networks, to cloud platforms and to the equipment suppliers who maintain them remotely. Sensors now feed vast quantities of data into analytical tools, and artificial intelligence is increasingly used to predict when a pump will fail, to optimise energy consumption or to adjust a production line in real time. The benefits are real: less downtime, lower costs and, in many cases, lower emissions.

The price, however, is a much larger attack surface. Many of the controllers still in service were designed fifteen or twenty years ago, when nobody imagined that they would one day be reachable from outside the plant. They often lack basic features such as authentication or encryption, and they cannot simply be switched off for an update, because stopping them may mean halting production for days. Security agencies have repeatedly warned that criminal groups and state-sponsored actors are probing these systems, and ransomware attacks have already forced manufacturers to shut down plants as a precaution.

Artificial intelligence cuts both ways in this contest. On the defensive side, machine-learning tools can learn what normal behaviour looks like on an industrial network and raise an alarm when a valve receives an unusual command at an unusual time. On the offensive side, the same techniques allow attackers to automate reconnaissance, write more convincing phishing messages and search for vulnerabilities at a speed no human team could match. There is also a newer risk: AI models embedded in control loops could themselves be manipulated, for example by feeding them deliberately distorted sensor data.

European legislators have responded on several fronts. The revised directive on network and information security, known as NIS2, has considerably widened the range of companies that must manage cyber risks and report serious incidents, including many manufacturers. The Cyber Resilience Act will require products with digital elements, from industrial routers to programmable controllers, to be designed securely and supported with updates throughout their life. And the Artificial Intelligence Act classifies AI used as a safety component in critical infrastructure as high-risk, with corresponding obligations on robustness and human oversight.

Experts agree, nonetheless, that regulation alone will not solve the problem. The decisive factor remains people. Industrial cybersecurity requires engineers who understand both the physics of the process and the logic of the network, and such profiles are scarce. Smaller suppliers, which form the backbone of European industry, often lack the resources to build that expertise in-house.

The lesson, as one industry report put it, is that safety and security can no longer be treated as separate disciplines. In a connected plant, a cyber incident is a safety incident.

keyPoints: Industrial control systems used to be isolated from the internet (the "air gap"), which was considered sufficient protection.

To gain efficiency they are now connected to corporate networks, cloud platforms and remote maintenance; AI is used for predictive maintenance, energy optimisation and real-time control, with real benefits.

This greatly enlarges the attack surface: legacy controllers lack authentication/encryption and cannot easily be stopped for updates; criminal and state-backed actors are probing them and ransomware has shut down plants.

AI cuts both ways: anomaly detection for defenders; automated reconnaissance, better phishing and faster vulnerability discovery for attackers; AI models in control loops can be manipulated with false sensor data.

EU response: NIS2 widens the companies that must manage cyber risks and report incidents; the Cyber Resilience Act requires secure-by-design products with updates; the AI Act treats AI safety components in critical infrastructure as high-risk.
Regulation is not enough: the shortage of engineers who understand both process and network is decisive, especially for smaller suppliers.
Conclusion: safety and security must be treated together; a cyber incident is a safety incident.

For decades these systems were protected by being physically isolated from the internet. Today, however, they are connected to corporate networks, cloud services and remote maintenance providers, and artificial intelligence is used to anticipate breakdowns, save energy and adjust production in real time, bringing clear economic and environmental benefits.

The downside is a far larger attack surface. Many controllers in use are decades old, lack authentication or encryption and cannot be easily taken offline for patching. Criminal and state-sponsored groups are actively targeting them, and ransomware has already forced plants to close temporarily. The EU has reacted with three instruments: NIS2, which extends risk-management and incident-reporting duties to many manufacturers; the Cyber Resilience Act, which requires secure, updatable digital products; and the AI Act, which classifies AI safety components in critical infrastructure as high-risk. Nevertheless, the author argues that the shortage of engineers combining process and IT knowledge, particularly in smaller firms, remains the key challenge, and that safety and security must now be managed as one.

spanish.title: El Gobierno presenta el Plan Nacional de Ciberseguridad Industrial
spanish.text:
El Ministerio de Industria y Turismo ha presentado hoy el Plan Nacional de Ciberseguridad Industrial, una hoja de ruta que tiene por objeto reforzar la protección de las instalaciones productivas frente a las amenazas digitales y acompañar a las empresas en la adaptación al nuevo marco normativo europeo. El Plan, elaborado en coordinación con los organismos competentes en materia de ciberseguridad y con las principales asociaciones empresariales, contará con una dotación de 150 millones de euros durante su período de vigencia.

La creciente interconexión de los sistemas de control industrial con las redes corporativas y con servicios en la nube ha incrementado de manera notable la exposición de la industria a los ciberataques. Según los datos del propio Ministerio, el número de incidentes notificados por empresas industriales se ha multiplicado en los últimos años, y una parte significativa de ellos ha obligado a paralizar total o parcialmente la producción.

El Plan se articula en torno a cuatro ejes. El primero consiste en la puesta en marcha de un programa de diagnóstico gratuito para pequeñas y medianas empresas, que permitirá evaluar su nivel de madurez en ciberseguridad y elaborar un plan de mejora personalizado. El segundo prevé una línea de ayudas para la adquisición de equipos y soluciones de protección, la segmentación de redes y la sustitución de componentes obsoletos que no admitan actualizaciones de seguridad.

El tercer eje se centra en la formación y la capacitación. Se impulsarán, en colaboración con universidades y centros de formación profesional, programas especializados que combinen conocimientos de automatización, procesos industriales y seguridad de la información, con el fin de paliar la escasez de profesionales con este perfil. El cuarto eje refuerza la cooperación público-privada mediante el intercambio de información sobre amenazas y vulnerabilidades y la realización periódica de ejercicios de simulación de incidentes.

Asimismo, el Plan contempla la adaptación de los reglamentos de seguridad industrial para incorporar requisitos de ciberseguridad en aquellas instalaciones en las que un incidente informático pueda afectar a la seguridad de las personas, los bienes o el medio ambiente, como las instalaciones de almacenamiento de productos químicos o los equipos a presión. Los organismos de control habilitados podrán verificar el cumplimiento de estos requisitos en el marco de las inspecciones periódicas.

Por último, el Ministerio facilitará guías prácticas para ayudar a las empresas a cumplir las obligaciones derivadas de la transposición de la Directiva NIS2, en particular las relativas a la gestión de riesgos, la notificación de incidentes significativos en los plazos establecidos y la seguridad de la cadena de suministro.

Durante la presentación, la secretaria general de Industria ha subrayado que la ciberseguridad ya no puede considerarse una cuestión exclusivamente tecnológica, sino un elemento esencial de la competitividad y de la continuidad de negocio. Ha añadido que la confianza de clientes e inversores depende cada vez más de la capacidad de las empresas para prevenir, detectar y responder a los ataques.

title: Simulacro IIE 4: congestión de redes e interconexiones / Ayudas al almacenamiento energético

listening.title: The forgotten backbone of the energy transition
listening.text:
When people picture the energy transition, they usually think of wind turbines on a ridge or solar panels stretching across a plain. They rarely think of pylons, cables and transformers. Yet the electricity grid is increasingly seen as the weakest link in Europe's decarbonisation strategy, and in several countries it has already become a brake on progress.

The problem can be summed up in one word: congestion. Renewable projects are being developed far faster than the networks needed to connect them. In some Member States, the volume of projects waiting for a grid connection exceeds the entire installed capacity of the country several times over. Industrial companies that wish to electrify their processes, data centres and charging hubs are also joining the queue, sometimes being told that a connection will not be available for many years.

Congestion has a cost even when the lights stay on. When the network cannot transport the electricity produced in windy or sunny regions to the places where it is consumed, system operators must order some generators to reduce their output and others to increase it elsewhere. This process, known as redispatch, costs European consumers several billion euros a year. At the same time, prices become negative in some hours, when there is simply more renewable power than the system can absorb.

Cross-border interconnections are a central part of the answer. A well-connected market allows surplus electricity in one country to replace more expensive generation in another, smoothing out the variability of wind and sun across a much larger area. The European Union has set a target for each Member State to have interconnection capacity equivalent to at least fifteen per cent of its installed generation capacity by 2030. Some countries are well above that level; others, notably on the periphery of the continent, remain far below it and function almost as energy islands.

The European Commission has estimated that several hundred billion euros of investment in distribution and transmission grids will be needed this decade alone. Its action plan for grids focuses on accelerating permitting, improving long-term network planning across borders, and encouraging regulators to allow anticipatory investment, that is, building capacity before every user has formally requested it. It also highlights the need to standardise equipment, since manufacturers of cables and transformers are struggling to keep up with demand and delivery times have lengthened considerably.

Not every solution requires new copper in the ground. Grid-enhancing technologies, such as sensors that measure the real-time capacity of a line depending on weather conditions, can squeeze more out of existing assets. Energy storage and demand flexibility can shift consumption to hours when the network is less loaded. And smarter connection rules, such as flexible connection agreements, can let new users connect sooner in exchange for accepting occasional limits.

None of this will happen without public acceptance. New power lines remain unpopular, and opposition from local communities can delay projects by years. If Europe wants its clean electricity to reach the factories and homes that need it, the grid must stop being an afterthought and become a political priority.

keyPoints: The grid, not generation, is increasingly the weakest link and a brake on decarbonisation.
Congestion: renewable projects and new demand (industry electrifying, data centres, charging hubs) wait years for connections; queues exceed national installed capacity in some countries.
Congestion is costly: redispatch costs consumers several billion euros a year, and prices turn negative when renewable output cannot be absorbed.
Interconnections spread variability over a larger area; EU target of at least 15% interconnection capacity by 2030; peripheral countries remain far below, almost energy islands.

Hundreds of billions of investment needed this decade; the EU grid action plan: faster permitting, cross-border planning, anticipatory investment, standardised equipment (supply-chain bottlenecks for cables and transformers).
Non-wire solutions: grid-enhancing technologies (dynamic line rating), storage, demand flexibility and flexible connection agreements.
Public acceptance is essential; the grid must become a political priority.

spanish.title: Convocatoria de ayudas para proyectos innovadores de almacenamiento energético
spanish.text:
El Ministerio para la Transición Ecológica y el Reto Demográfico, a través del Instituto para la Diversificación y Ahorro de la Energía (IDAE), ha abierto una nueva convocatoria de ayudas destinada a proyectos de almacenamiento energético, con un presupuesto de 200 millones de euros. La iniciativa responde a la necesidad de dotar al sistema eléctrico de mayor flexibilidad ante la creciente penetración de las energías renovables y de reducir los vertidos de energía que se producen en las horas de mayor generación.

Podrán acogerse a las ayudas tres tipologías de proyectos. En primer lugar, las instalaciones de almacenamiento independientes conectadas directamente a la red, tanto de transporte como de distribución. En segundo lugar, los sistemas de almacenamiento hibridados con instalaciones de generación renovable existentes o de nueva construcción, que compartan punto de conexión. En tercer lugar, el almacenamiento térmico asociado a instalaciones de generación termosolar, así como las nuevas centrales hidroeléctricas de bombeo o la ampliación de las existentes.

Las tecnologías subvencionables incluyen, entre otras, las baterías electroquímicas, el bombeo hidráulico, el almacenamiento térmico en sales fundidas y otras soluciones innovadoras, siempre que garanticen una capacidad de almacenamiento mínima equivalente a dos horas de funcionamiento a potencia nominal. Se valorarán especialmente los proyectos que contribuyan a resolver restricciones técnicas en zonas con elevada congestión de la red.

Las ayudas se concederán en régimen de concurrencia competitiva y adoptarán la forma de subvención a fondo perdido. La intensidad máxima dependerá del tamaño de la empresa beneficiaria y de la tecnología empleada, y no podrá superar en ningún caso los límites establecidos en el Reglamento general de exención por categorías. Los criterios de valoración tendrán en cuenta el importe de ayuda solicitado por unidad de capacidad, la viabilidad técnica y económica del proyecto, su grado de madurez y su contribución a la cadena de valor industrial en España.

Para poder participar, los solicitantes deberán disponer, en el momento de presentar la solicitud, de los permisos de acceso y conexión a la red o, en su defecto, acreditar haberlos solicitado. Asimismo, deberán presentar un plan de desmantelamiento y gestión de residuos al final de la vida útil de la instalación, que garantice el reciclaje de los componentes y, en particular, la recuperación de las materias primas fundamentales contenidas en las baterías.

El plazo de presentación de solicitudes será de tres meses a partir del día siguiente a la publicación del extracto de la convocatoria. Las instalaciones deberán estar en funcionamiento en un plazo máximo de treinta meses desde la resolución definitiva de concesión, salvo en el caso de las centrales de bombeo, cuyo plazo se ampliará atendiendo a la complejidad de su tramitación ambiental.

Según el Ministerio, el almacenamiento será una pieza clave para alcanzar los objetivos del Plan Nacional Integrado de Energía y Clima, que prevé un aumento muy significativo de la capacidad de almacenamiento a lo largo de la presente década, y contribuirá a reforzar la seguridad de suministro y la estabilidad del sistema eléctrico.

Call for aid for innovative energy storage projects

The Ministry for the Ecological Transition and the Demographic Challenge, through the Institute for Energy Diversification and Saving (IDAE), has opened a new call for aid for energy storage projects, with a budget of 200 million euros. The initiative responds to the need to make the electricity system more flexible in the face of the growing penetration of renewable energy and to reduce the curtailment of energy that occurs during the hours of highest generation.

Three types of project will be eligible for aid. First, stand-alone storage facilities connected directly to the grid, whether to the transmission or the distribution network. Second, storage systems hybridised with existing or new renewable generation plants and sharing their connection point. Third, thermal storage associated with solar thermal power plants, as well as new pumped-storage hydropower plants or the expansion of existing ones.

Eligible technologies include, among others, electrochemical batteries, pumped hydro, molten-salt thermal storage and other innovative solutions, provided that they guarantee a minimum storage capacity equivalent to two hours of operation at rated power. Particular weight will be given to projects that help to resolve technical constraints in areas with high grid congestion.

The aid will be awarded through a competitive procedure and will take the form of non-repayable grants. The maximum aid intensity will depend on the size of the beneficiary company and the technology used, and may under no circumstances exceed the limits laid down in the General Block Exemption Regulation. The assessment criteria will take into account the amount of aid requested per unit of capacity, the technical and economic viability of the project, its degree of maturity and its contribution to the industrial value chain in Spain.

In order to take part, applicants must hold, at the time of application, grid access and connection permits or, failing that, provide evidence that they have applied for them. They must also submit a plan for decommissioning and waste management at the end of the facility's service life, ensuring that components are recycled and, in particular, that the critical raw materials contained in the batteries are recovered.

Applications may be submitted for three months from the day following the publication of the summary of the call. Facilities must be in operation within a maximum of thirty months from the final award decision, except for pumped-storage plants, for which the deadline will be extended in view of the complexity of their environmental permitting procedure.

According to the Ministry, storage will be a key element in meeting the targets of the National Integrated Energy and Climate Plan, which foresees a very significant increase in storage capacity over the current decade, and will help to strengthen security of supply and the stability of the electricity system.

listening.title: Mining the cities: can recycling secure Europe's critical raw materials?
listening.text:
Somewhere in a drawer in almost every European home lies a small treasure that nobody thinks about: an old mobile phone. It contains copper and gold, but also cobalt, lithium, tantalum, rare earth elements and a dozen other metals that the European Union now classifies as critical or strategic. Multiply that drawer by hundreds of millions of households, add the discarded laptops, electric bicycles, wind turbine magnets and, increasingly, electric vehicle batteries, and you begin to see why some experts describe our cities as the mines of the future.

The idea of urban mining is simple. Instead of digging new ore out of the ground, we recover metals from products that have reached the end of their life. In some cases, the concentrations are remarkable: a tonne of discarded circuit boards can contain considerably more gold than a tonne of ore from a typical gold mine. Recycling also tends to use far less energy than primary production, generates less waste rock and avoids many of the land-use conflicts that make new mining projects so difficult to approve in Europe.

The reality, however, is less encouraging than the theory. According to international monitoring reports, the world now generates more than sixty million tonnes of electronic waste every year, and less than a quarter of it is formally collected and recycled. The rest ends up in landfills, in informal workshops where metals are recovered in dangerous conditions, or simply stays in our drawers. Even when devices are collected, the recovery rate for many critical elements is extremely low. For rare earths, the share obtained from recycling is still in the low single digits, because the metals are present in tiny quantities, mixed with plastics and other materials, and difficult to separate economically.

There is also a more fundamental limitation. Recycling can only return what was put into circulation years or decades earlier. When demand is growing rapidly, as it is for lithium, nickel and rare earths driven by electric vehicles and renewable energy, the volume of material reaching the end of its life is necessarily much smaller than the volume needed today. Even with perfect recycling, primary mining would still be required for at least the next two decades. Urban mining is therefore a complement to conventional mining, not a substitute for it.

The European Union has nonetheless made recycling a central pillar of its Critical Raw Materials Act. Alongside benchmarks for domestic extraction and processing, the Act sets the objective that, by 2030, recycling should be able to cover a quarter of the Union's annual consumption of strategic raw materials. It also states that no more than sixty-five per cent of the Union's consumption of any strategic raw material, at any relevant stage of processing, should come from a single third country. Recycling projects can be designated as strategic projects, which gives them access to faster permitting and to support in finding finance.

Other rules reinforce this approach. The new Batteries Regulation sets minimum levels of recycled content for cobalt, lithium, nickel and lead in new industrial and electric vehicle batteries, and minimum recovery rates for the materials in waste batteries. Manufacturers of products containing permanent magnets will have to provide information on their composition and on how they can be removed. The aim is to create a guaranteed market for secondary materials, which have historically struggled to compete with cheap primary metals whose prices fluctuate wildly.

Technology is moving quickly. Hydrometallurgical processes, which dissolve metals in chemical solutions and then separate them selectively, can now recover more than ninety per cent of the cobalt and nickel in lithium-ion batteries. Researchers are developing methods to recover rare earths from magnets without fully dissolving them, and automated disassembly lines using robotics and machine vision promise to make the dismantling of complex products cheaper. Yet many of these technologies remain at pilot scale, and Europe still sends a considerable share of its battery waste, in the form of so-called black mass, to be processed in Asia.

The obstacles are as much economic and organisational as they are technical. Collection systems need to be convenient for citizens. Products need to be designed from the outset to be repaired and dismantled. And recyclers need investment certainty, which is difficult when the value of what they recover depends on volatile commodity prices.

If these challenges can be overcome, the rewards are considerable: a more secure supply of essential materials, lower emissions and fewer environmental impacts. The mines of the future may indeed be in our cities, but only if we learn how to work them.

keyPoints: Discarded electronics, magnets and batteries contain critical and strategic metals; cities can be seen as "mines of the future" (urban mining).
Advantages: high concentrations (more gold per tonne of circuit boards than in ore), lower energy use, less waste and fewer land-use conflicts than new mines.

Reality: over 60 million tonnes of e-waste a year, under a quarter formally recycled; recovery of many critical elements (e.g. rare earths) remains very low because they are dispersed and hard to separate.
Fundamental limit: with rapidly rising demand, end-of-life material cannot meet current needs; primary mining remains necessary for at least two decades; recycling complements mining.

Critical Raw Materials Act: by 2030 recycling should cover 25% of annual EU consumption of strategic raw materials; no more than 65% from a single third country; recycling projects can be strategic projects with faster permits and financing support.
Batteries Regulation: minimum recycled content (cobalt, lithium, nickel, lead) and recovery rates; information requirements for permanent magnets; aim to guarantee a market for secondary materials.
Technology: hydrometallurgy recovers over 90% of cobalt and nickel; new rare-earth recovery methods and robotic disassembly, but many are at pilot scale and much black mass is processed in Asia.
Remaining obstacles: collection, design for repair and dismantling, investment certainty amid volatile prices; rewards are security of supply and lower environmental impact.
modelSummary:
The text explores the potential and limits of urban mining, the recovery of critical metals from end-of-life products. Old phones, computers, magnets and batteries contain metals such as cobalt, lithium and rare earths, sometimes in higher concentrations than natural ores, and recycling them generally requires less energy and causes fewer conflicts than opening new mines.

In practice, however, less than a quarter of the more than 60 million tonnes of electronic waste generated annually is formally recycled, and recovery rates for elements like rare earths remain minimal because they are dispersed and hard to separate. Moreover, since demand for battery and renewable-energy materials is growing fast, recycled supply cannot keep pace, so primary mining will remain indispensable for decades; recycling is a complement, not an alternative.

The EU has nonetheless placed recycling at the heart of the Critical Raw Materials Act, aiming for it to cover 25% of strategic raw material consumption by 2030, limiting dependence on any single third country to 65% and offering strategic recycling projects faster permits. The Batteries Regulation adds recycled-content and recovery targets to create a stable market for secondary materials.

Although hydrometallurgy and robotic dismantling are making progress, many solutions are still at pilot scale and much battery waste is processed in Asia. Better collection, design for dismantling and investment certainty are needed if urban mining is to strengthen supply security.

spanish.title: El Gobierno agiliza la tramitación de los derechos mineros vinculados a proyectos estratégicos
spanish.text:
El Consejo de Ministros ha aprobado, a propuesta del Ministerio para la Transición Ecológica y el Reto Demográfico, un real decreto por el que se modifica el Reglamento General para el Régimen de la Minería con el fin de adaptar la tramitación de los derechos mineros a las exigencias derivadas del Reglamento europeo de materias primas fundamentales. La norma pretende reducir los plazos administrativos sin menoscabo de las garantías ambientales ni de la participación pública.

El citado Reglamento europeo establece que los procedimientos de concesión de autorizaciones para los proyectos declarados estratégicos no podrán superar los veintisiete meses en el caso de los proyectos de extracción y los quince meses en el caso de los proyectos de transformación o reciclado. Para dar cumplimiento a estas previsiones, el real decreto designa a la Dirección General de Política Energética y Minas como punto único de contacto, que coordinará a todas las administraciones que intervienen en el procedimiento y actuará como interlocutor del promotor.

Entre las principales novedades, se establece la tramitación preferente y simultánea de los permisos de investigación, de las concesiones de explotación derivadas y de las autorizaciones sectoriales necesarias, de forma que la evaluación de impacto ambiental pueda desarrollarse en paralelo y no de manera sucesiva. Asimismo, se prevé la posibilidad de celebrar reuniones previas con el promotor para delimitar el alcance de la documentación exigible y evitar requerimientos posteriores que dilaten innecesariamente el procedimiento.

La norma refuerza también los requisitos técnicos exigidos a los solicitantes. Los proyectos deberán incluir un estudio de viabilidad que acredite la existencia de un recurso económicamente explotable, un plan de labores detallado y un plan de restauración del espacio natural afectado, acompañado de la correspondiente garantía financiera. Además, deberán describir las medidas previstas para minimizar el consumo de agua y energía y para gestionar de forma segura los residuos mineros, incluidas las instalaciones de residuos.

En materia de transparencia, el real decreto obliga a publicar en la sede electrónica del Ministerio la información relativa al estado de tramitación de cada expediente y garantiza la participación de las entidades locales y de la ciudadanía en las fases de información pública. Las comunidades autónomas, competentes en la mayoría de los casos para el otorgamiento de los derechos mineros, podrán suscribir convenios de colaboración con la Administración General del Estado para la tramitación coordinada de los proyectos que afecten a su territorio.

El Ministerio subraya que España cuenta con un potencial geológico relevante en materias primas consideradas fundamentales, como el litio, el wolframio, el cobre, la fluorita o el grafito, y que el aprovechamiento responsable de estos recursos puede contribuir a la autonomía estratégica de la Unión Europea y a la creación de empleo en zonas rurales, a menudo afectadas por la despoblación.

No obstante, la norma insiste en que la declaración de un proyecto como estratégico no exime en ningún caso del cumplimiento de la legislación ambiental, ni supone la autorización automática del proyecto. Las administraciones competentes deberán resolver de forma motivada y podrán denegar la autorización cuando el proyecto no cumpla los requisitos exigidos o resulte incompatible con la protección de espacios naturales o de recursos hídricos.

El real decreto entrará en vigor el día siguiente al de su publicación en el Boletín Oficial del Estado y será de aplicación a los procedimientos que se inicien a partir de esa fecha.

The Council of Ministers, at the proposal of the Ministry for the Ecological Transition and the Demographic Challenge, has approved a royal decree amending the General Regulation on the Mining Regime in order to adapt the processing of mining rights to the requirements arising from the European Critical Raw Materials Regulation. The new rules seek to shorten administrative deadlines without weakening environmental safeguards or public participation.

The European Regulation provides that permit-granting procedures for projects designated as strategic may not exceed twenty-seven months for extraction projects and fifteen months for processing or recycling projects. To comply with these provisions, the royal decree designates the Directorate-General for Energy and Mining Policy as the single point of contact, which will coordinate all the authorities involved in the procedure and act as the developer's point of reference.

Among the main new features, the decree establishes the priority and simultaneous processing of exploration permits, the resulting mining concessions and the necessary sectoral authorisations, so that the environmental impact assessment can be carried out in parallel rather than sequentially. It also provides for the possibility of holding preliminary meetings with the developer to define the scope of the required documentation and avoid subsequent requests for information that unnecessarily prolong the procedure.

The decree also strengthens the technical requirements for applicants. Projects must include a feasibility study demonstrating the existence of an economically exploitable resource, a detailed mining plan and a plan for the rehabilitation of the affected natural area, together with the corresponding financial guarantee. In addition, they must describe the measures planned to minimise water and energy consumption and to manage extractive waste safely, including waste facilities.

As regards transparency, the royal decree requires information on the processing status of each application to be published on the Ministry's electronic office and guarantees the participation of local authorities and citizens during the public consultation stages. The autonomous communities, which are responsible for granting mining rights in most cases, may sign cooperation agreements with the General State Administration for the coordinated processing of projects affecting their territory.

The Ministry stresses that Spain has significant geological potential in raw materials considered critical, such as lithium, tungsten, copper, fluorspar and graphite, and that the responsible use of these resources can contribute to the strategic autonomy of the European Union and to job creation in rural areas, which are often affected by depopulation.

However, the decree insists that designating a project as strategic in no way exempts it from compliance with environmental legislation, nor does it entail automatic approval of the project. The competent authorities must give reasoned decisions and may refuse authorisation where the project does not meet the requirements or is incompatible with the protection of natural areas or water resources.

The royal decree will enter into force on the day following its publication in the Official State Gazette and will apply to procedures initiated from that date.

listening.title: Every drop counts: why water is becoming mining's defining challenge
listening.text:
For most of its history, the mining industry has treated water as a practical problem rather than a strategic one. Water was something to be pumped out of a pit so that work could continue, or something to be brought in to process ore and suppress dust. Its cost was low, its availability was rarely questioned and the consequences of its misuse were often felt far away and long after a mine had closed.

That attitude is changing rapidly, and for good reason. A large proportion of the world's copper, lithium and gold is produced in regions that already suffer from water stress, from the high deserts of South America to parts of Australia, southern Africa and the Mediterranean basin. As the energy transition drives up demand for these metals, mines are competing for the same scarce resource as farmers, cities and fragile ecosystems. In several countries, disputes over water have become the main reason why new projects are delayed or rejected, ahead of concerns about land, noise or even employment.

The industry's response has been gathered under a single term: water stewardship. The concept goes beyond simple compliance with discharge limits. It means understanding the entire catchment in which a mine operates, measuring every flow of water entering and leaving the site, sharing that information with local communities and regulators, and taking responsibility for the cumulative effects of mining alongside those of other users. Industry bodies have published guidance encouraging companies to report not only how much water they withdraw, but also where it comes from, how much is recycled and how much quality is lost along the way.

Technically, the options are well known. The most immediate is to reuse process water as many times as possible. Modern concentrators can recycle a large majority of the water they use, recovering it from thickeners and tailings before it is lost. A second option is to change how tailings, the finely ground waste left after processing, are stored. Conventional tailings dams hold enormous volumes of water, much of which evaporates or seeps into the ground. Filtered or so-called dry-stacked tailings, by contrast, are dewatered before deposition, which saves water and also reduces the risk of catastrophic dam failure, a risk that the world was forced to confront after several tragic collapses in recent years.

A third option, increasingly common in arid coastal regions, is to use seawater, either directly in some processes or after desalination. This relieves pressure on freshwater aquifers, but it comes at a price. Desalination consumes large amounts of energy, and when the water must be pumped hundreds of kilometres inland and several thousand metres uphill, the costs and emissions rise considerably. The use of renewable electricity can mitigate the climate impact, but not the capital investment involved.

Water quality is just as important as quantity. When sulphide minerals in waste rock and tailings are exposed to air and water, they can generate acid mine drainage, a highly acidic solution that dissolves heavy metals and can contaminate rivers and groundwater for decades, sometimes centuries. Preventing it requires careful design from the very first day of operation: isolating reactive material, covering it to limit oxygen ingress and, where necessary, treating drainage through active chemical plants or passive systems such as constructed wetlands.

Perhaps the most significant shift, however, is cultural. Increasingly, investors, insurers and buyers of metals want evidence that the materials they purchase have been produced responsibly. Water performance now features in sustainability ratings, in the due diligence requirements imposed by new European legislation and in the conditions attached to finance. A mine that cannot demonstrate a credible water strategy may find it harder to secure capital, regardless of the quality of its ore body.

The challenge for regulators is to translate these principles into enforceable rules without discouraging investment. That means setting clear standards for water balances and discharge quality, requiring robust monitoring that continues long after closure and ensuring that financial guarantees are sufficient to cover long-term water treatment. In the end, a mine is a temporary activity, but its impact on water can be permanent. Recognising that asymmetry is the starting point of genuine stewardship.

spanish.title: Nuevas exigencias para la restauración de los espacios afectados por actividades mineras
spanish.text:
El Ministerio para la Transición Ecológica y el Reto Demográfico ha sometido a información pública el proyecto de real decreto por el que se modifica la normativa sobre gestión de los residuos de las industrias extractivas y de protección y rehabilitación del espacio afectado por actividades mineras. La reforma tiene como finalidad reforzar las garantías de que los terrenos afectados por la minería recuperen, una vez finalizada la explotación, un uso compatible con su entorno natural y socioeconómico.

La experiencia acumulada en las últimas décadas pone de manifiesto que la restauración no puede abordarse como una fase final y aislada, sino que debe integrarse desde el inicio en el diseño del proyecto. Por ello, el texto exige que el plan de restauración se presente junto con la solicitud de autorización o concesión, que contemple la restauración progresiva a medida que avanzan las labores y que sea revisado periódicamente, al menos cada cinco años, para adaptarlo a la evolución real de la explotación.

El plan deberá incluir, entre otros aspectos, una caracterización detallada del estado inicial del terreno, de los suelos, de la vegetación y de las aguas superficiales y subterráneas; la descripción de las medidas de remodelado topográfico y de estabilización de taludes; las actuaciones de revegetación con especies autóctonas; y un programa de seguimiento y control que se prolongará tras el cierre durante el tiempo necesario para verificar el éxito de la rehabilitación.

Especial atención merecen las instalaciones de residuos mineros, como escombreras y balsas de lodos. El proyecto de real decreto obliga a clasificar estas instalaciones en función de su riesgo, a realizar inspecciones periódicas de su estabilidad y a disponer de un plan de emergencia interior en aquellas que puedan dar lugar a un accidente grave. Asimismo, se exigirá prevenir la formación de drenajes ácidos y, en caso de que se produzcan, garantizar su tratamiento hasta que la calidad de las aguas sea compatible con los objetivos ambientales de la masa de agua receptora.

Uno de los cambios más relevantes afecta a la garantía financiera, que deberá cubrir en todo momento el coste íntegro de las labores de rehabilitación pendientes, calculado como si estas tuvieran que ser ejecutadas por un tercero independiente. La garantía se actualizará con la revisión del plan y no podrá liberarse, ni siquiera parcialmente, hasta que la autoridad competente haya comprobado sobre el terreno la correcta ejecución de los trabajos. De este modo se pretende evitar que el coste de la restauración recaiga sobre las administraciones públicas en caso de abandono o insolvencia de la empresa.

El texto también promueve usos posteriores innovadores de los espacios restaurados, siempre que sean compatibles con la seguridad y el medio ambiente. Entre ellos figuran la creación de humedales y espacios de interés para la biodiversidad, el aprovechamiento agrícola o forestal, la instalación de plantas de energía renovable o el aprovechamiento de huecos mineros como depósitos para el almacenamiento de agua o de energía mediante bombeo.

Por último, se crea un inventario de explotaciones mineras abandonadas que presenten riesgos para la seguridad o el medio ambiente, con el fin de priorizar las actuaciones de las administraciones en función de su peligrosidad. Las comunidades autónomas, competentes en materia de autorización y control de la restauración, deberán remitir anualmente la información necesaria para mantener actualizado dicho inventario.

El plazo para presentar alegaciones será de cuarenta y cinco días hábiles a partir de la publicación del anuncio en el portal de participación pública del Ministerio.

New requirements for the rehabilitation of areas affected by mining activities

The Ministry for the Ecological Transition and the Demographic Challenge has opened a public consultation on the draft royal decree amending the regulations on the management of waste from extractive industries and on the protection and rehabilitation of areas affected by mining activities. The purpose of the reform is to provide stronger guarantees that land affected by mining will, once operations have ended, regain a use compatible with its natural and socio-economic surroundings.

Experience gained over recent decades shows that rehabilitation cannot be treated as a final, isolated stage, but must be built into the design of the project from the outset. The draft therefore requires the rehabilitation plan to be submitted together with the application for authorisation or a concession, to provide for progressive rehabilitation as the works advance, and to be reviewed periodically, at least every five years, so as to adapt it to the actual development of the operation.

The plan must include, among other aspects, a detailed characterisation of the initial condition of the land, soils, vegetation and surface water and groundwater; a description of the measures for landform reshaping and slope stabilisation; revegetation with native species; and a monitoring and control programme that will continue after closure for as long as necessary to verify that the rehabilitation has been successful.

Extractive waste facilities, such as waste rock dumps and tailings ponds, warrant particular attention. The draft royal decree requires these facilities to be classified according to their risk, their stability to be inspected periodically and an internal emergency plan to be in place for those that could give rise to a major accident. Operators will also be required to prevent acid drainage and, should it occur, to ensure that it is treated until water quality is compatible with the environmental objectives of the receiving water body.

One of the most significant changes concerns the financial guarantee, which must at all times cover the full cost of the outstanding rehabilitation works, calculated as if they had to be carried out by an independent third party. The guarantee will be updated whenever the plan is reviewed and may not be released, even partially, until the competent authority has verified on site that the works have been properly carried out. The aim is to prevent the cost of rehabilitation from falling on public authorities if the company abandons the site or becomes insolvent.

The text also encourages innovative after-uses of rehabilitated sites, provided they are compatible with safety and the environment. These include the creation of wetlands and areas of interest for biodiversity, agricultural or forestry use, the installation of renewable energy plants, and the use of mine voids as reservoirs for water storage or for pumped energy storage.

Finally, an inventory is to be created of abandoned mines that pose risks to safety or the environment, in order to prioritise the authorities' interventions according to the level of hazard. The autonomous communities, which are responsible for authorising and supervising rehabilitation, will have to submit the information needed to keep this inventory up to date every year.

Comments may be submitted within forty-five working days of the publication of the notice on the Ministry's public participation portal.

title: Simulacro Minas 3: geotermia profunda / Seguridad en voladuras y normativa de explosivos

listening.title: The heat beneath our feet
listening.text:
Beneath every square metre of the European continent lies a vast and almost inexhaustible source of energy. The temperature of the Earth's crust rises, on average, by around three degrees Celsius for every hundred metres of depth. At four or five kilometres below the surface, the rock is hot enough almost everywhere to heat buildings, and in many places hot enough to generate electricity. Unlike wind and solar power, this heat is available day and night, in every season, regardless of the weather. And yet geothermal energy still supplies only a tiny fraction of Europe's energy needs.

Why has such a promising resource remained on the margins? The answer lies largely in geology and economics. Conventional geothermal power depends on a fortunate combination of conditions: high temperatures relatively close to the surface, permeable rock and abundant natural fluids. Such conditions are found in volcanic regions such as Iceland, parts of Italy or Turkey, but they are the exception rather than the rule. Elsewhere, developers must drill much deeper, and drilling is expensive. A single deep well can cost several million euros, and the developer only discovers whether the reservoir is productive once the well has been completed. This exploration risk has deterred private investors for decades.

Nevertheless, several developments suggest that geothermal energy may be on the verge of a breakthrough. The first comes, somewhat ironically, from the oil and gas industry. Techniques developed to extract hydrocarbons, such as horizontal drilling, multi-stage stimulation and advanced seismic imaging, are now being adapted to geothermal projects. Some recent pilot projects have managed to drill wells in hard, hot granite far faster and more cheaply than was thought possible only a few years ago, and drilling costs appear to be falling as the industry gains experience.

The second development is the emergence of so-called enhanced or engineered geothermal systems. Instead of searching for a rare natural reservoir, engineers create one by injecting water under pressure to open up small fractures in hot, dry rock. Cold water is then pumped down one well, circulates through the fractured rock, absorbs heat and returns to the surface through another well. In principle, this approach could make geothermal power possible almost anywhere. A related concept, the closed-loop system, circulates fluid through sealed pipes deep underground, avoiding contact with the rock altogether, although it extracts heat more slowly.

The third development concerns demand. Industry needs enormous quantities of heat, much of it at temperatures between one hundred and two hundred degrees, for processes such as drying, food production, paper making and chemicals. Geothermal energy is well suited to supply this heat directly, without converting it to electricity first. District heating networks, already widespread in northern and central Europe, offer another natural outlet, and several European cities are now drilling deep wells to replace gas-fired boilers.

The obstacles, however, should not be underestimated. Stimulating rock at depth can trigger small earthquakes. Most are imperceptible, but a few projects in Europe have caused tremors strong enough to be felt by residents and to damage buildings, leading to their suspension or permanent closure. Today, operators rely on detailed seismic monitoring and so-called traffic-light protocols, which require injection to be reduced or halted if seismic activity exceeds predefined thresholds. Geothermal fluids may also contain dissolved gases and minerals that must be managed carefully, and public acceptance cannot be taken for granted.

Regulation is another hurdle. In many countries, the subsurface is governed by mining legislation that was written with minerals in mind, not heat. Licensing procedures can be slow and unclear, and responsibilities are often divided among several authorities. The European Union has recognised geothermal energy as a renewable source eligible for accelerated permitting in designated areas, and has called on Member States to remove administrative barriers and to establish risk-sharing schemes that would cover part of the cost of an unsuccessful well.

Spain is an interesting case. Despite having areas of considerable geothermal potential, including the Canary Islands and several sedimentary basins on the mainland, the country has barely begun to exploit its deep resources. Geological surveys and pilot drilling programmes could change this, provided that the regulatory framework offers developers clarity and that the lessons learned elsewhere on induced seismicity are taken seriously. The heat is there. The question is whether Europe will find the will and the instruments to bring it to the surface.

Barriers: conventional geothermal needs rare conditions (volcanic regions); deep drilling is expensive (several million euros per well) and exploration risk deters investors.
Breakthrough factors: oil and gas techniques (horizontal drilling, multi-stage stimulation, seismic imaging) are cutting drilling time and costs.
Enhanced/engineered geothermal systems create artificial reservoirs by fracturing hot dry rock; closed-loop systems circulate fluid in sealed pipes (no rock contact, slower heat extraction).
Demand: industrial heat at 100-200 °C and district heating networks are natural markets; cities are drilling to replace gas boilers.
Risks: induced seismicity has led to suspensions or closures; managed with seismic monitoring and traffic-light protocols; fluids contain gases/minerals; public acceptance not guaranteed.
Regulation: mining laws not designed for heat, slow licensing, fragmented responsibilities; EU supports accelerated permitting and calls for risk-sharing schemes for failed wells.
Spain has potential (Canary Islands, sedimentary basins) but little development; needs surveys, pilot drilling and a clear framework.
