The text examines why deep geothermal energy, a constant and weather-independent resource available beneath almost all of Europe, still makes only a marginal contribution to the energy mix, and why this may be about to change.

Conventional geothermal power requires high temperatures, permeable rock and natural fluids near the surface, conditions largely restricted to volcanic areas. Elsewhere, wells must be very deep and costly, and the risk that a well proves unproductive has long discouraged investment.

Three trends, however, point to a possible breakthrough. First, oil and gas drilling techniques are being transferred to geothermal projects, reducing drilling times and costs. Second, enhanced geothermal systems create artificial reservoirs by fracturing hot, dry rock, while closed-loop designs circulate fluid in sealed pipes, potentially making geothermal viable almost anywhere. Third, there is strong demand for medium-temperature industrial heat and for district heating, which geothermal can supply directly.

Significant obstacles remain. Rock stimulation can induce earthquakes, some of which have forced projects to close, so operators now use seismic monitoring and traffic-light protocols. Fluids must be carefully managed and public acceptance secured. Moreover, mining-based regulations are often ill-suited to heat extraction, prompting the EU to promote faster permitting and risk-sharing schemes. The text concludes that Spain, despite promising resources, has barely begun to develop them and needs a clear regulatory framework.

spanish.title: Refuerzo de la seguridad en las voladuras y en el uso de explosivos con fines civiles
spanish.text:
El Ministerio de Industria y Turismo, en coordinación con el Ministerio del Interior, ha aprobado una orden por la que se actualizan diversas instrucciones técnicas complementarias relativas a la seguridad en el empleo de explosivos en explotaciones mineras, obras públicas y demoliciones. La revisión responde a la evolución tecnológica del sector, en particular a la generalización de los detonadores electrónicos, y a la necesidad de reforzar la protección de los trabajadores, de las poblaciones cercanas y del medio ambiente.

La norma establece que toda voladura deberá ejecutarse conforme a un proyecto de voladura aprobado por la autoridad minera competente, en el que se definan, entre otros aspectos, el esquema de perforación, la carga de explosivo por barreno, la secuencia de iniciación y el radio de seguridad. Cuando la voladura se realice en las proximidades de núcleos urbanos, infraestructuras o bienes protegidos, el proyecto deberá incluir un estudio de vibraciones y de onda aérea que acredite que no se superarán los valores límite establecidos.

Asimismo, se refuerzan las obligaciones relativas a la cualificación del personal. Únicamente podrán manipular explosivos y efectuar las operaciones de carga y disparo los artilleros que estén en posesión de la cartilla correspondiente en vigor, expedida tras la superación de un curso de formación específico y de un examen. La cartilla deberá renovarse periódicamente, y su titular estará obligado a seguir cursos de actualización cuando se introduzcan nuevas técnicas o productos.

En lo que se refiere al almacenamiento, los depósitos de explosivos deberán contar con la autorización previa de la Delegación del Gobierno y cumplir las distancias mínimas de seguridad a edificaciones y vías de comunicación, así como disponer de sistemas de vigilancia y de control de accesos. El transporte de explosivos hasta el lugar de consumo se ajustará a lo dispuesto en la normativa sobre transporte de mercancías peligrosas por carretera, y la cantidad transportada no podrá exceder de la necesaria para la jornada de trabajo.

La orden incide de manera especial en la trazabilidad. Todos los explosivos y detonadores deberán estar identificados mediante un código único que permita conocer en todo momento su origen y destino, desde su fabricación hasta su uso final. Los consumidores habituales deberán llevar un libro registro de los productos recibidos, consumidos y devueltos, que estará a disposición de la Guardia Civil y de la autoridad minera, y comunicar de inmediato cualquier pérdida o sustracción.

En cuanto a la ejecución de las voladuras, se exige la delimitación y el control de la zona de seguridad, la emisión de señales acústicas reglamentarias antes y después del disparo y la comprobación, una vez transcurrido el tiempo de espera, de que no han quedado barrenos fallidos. En caso de detectarse alguno, se prohíbe expresamente volver a perforar en sus proximidades y se deberá proceder a su neutralización conforme al procedimiento establecido en el proyecto.

Por último, la orden prevé que las empresas que utilicen explosivos designen a un director facultativo responsable de la seguridad de las operaciones, e incorporen la evaluación de los riesgos derivados de las voladuras en su documento sobre seguridad y salud. Las inspecciones periódicas comprobarán el cumplimiento de estas medidas, y su incumplimiento podrá dar lugar a la suspensión inmediata de los trabajos.

Stronger safety measures for blasting and the use of explosives for civil purposes

The Ministry of Industry and Tourism, in coordination with the Ministry of the Interior, has approved an order updating a number of supplementary technical instructions on safety in the use of explosives in mines, public works and demolition. The revision responds to technological developments in the sector, in particular the widespread use of electronic detonators, and to the need to provide greater protection for workers, nearby communities and the environment.

The order stipulates that every blast must be carried out in accordance with a blasting design approved by the competent mining authority, which must specify, among other aspects, the drilling pattern, the explosive charge per hole, the initiation sequence and the safety radius. Where blasting takes place near built-up areas, infrastructure or protected property, the design must include a ground vibration and air blast study demonstrating that the established limit values will not be exceeded.

The obligations relating to staff qualifications are also tightened. Only shotfirers holding a valid licence, issued after completing a specific training course and passing an examination, may handle explosives and carry out charging and firing operations. The licence must be renewed periodically, and its holder will be required to attend refresher courses whenever new techniques or products are introduced.

As regards storage, explosives magazines must have prior authorisation from the Government Delegation and comply with minimum safety distances from buildings and transport routes, as well as having surveillance and access control systems. The transport of explosives to the place of use must comply with the regulations on the carriage of dangerous goods by road, and the quantity transported may not exceed that needed for the working day.

The order places particular emphasis on traceability. All explosives and detonators must be identified by a unique code making it possible to know their origin and destination at all times, from manufacture to final use. Regular users must keep a register of the products received, used and returned, which must be made available to the Guardia Civil and the mining authority, and must immediately report any loss or theft.

With regard to the execution of blasts, the safety zone must be marked out and controlled, the statutory audible warnings must be given before and after firing and, once the waiting time has elapsed, it must be checked that there are no misfired holes. If any are detected, drilling in their vicinity is expressly prohibited and they must be neutralised in accordance with the procedure laid down in the blasting design.

Finally, the order requires companies using explosives to appoint a technical manager responsible for the safety of operations and to include the assessment of blasting-related risks in their health and safety document. Periodic inspections will check compliance with these measures, and failure to comply may lead to the immediate suspension of works.

title: Simulacro Minas 4: almacenamiento geológico de CO2 / Hidrógeno y almacenamiento subterráneo

listening.title: Putting carbon back underground
listening.text:
For more than a century, industrial societies have been taking carbon out of the ground in the form of coal, oil and gas, and releasing it into the atmosphere. The idea of reversing part of that journey, by capturing carbon dioxide and returning it to deep geological formations, has been discussed for decades. Until recently, however, it remained largely confined to research projects and a handful of pioneering sites. That is now beginning to change.

The reason is simple. Even in the most ambitious climate scenarios, some industrial emissions are extremely difficult to avoid by other means. In cement production, roughly two thirds of the carbon dioxide released comes not from burning fuel but from the chemical transformation of limestone into lime. Similar process emissions arise in lime production, in some chemical plants and in waste incineration. For these sectors, capturing the gas and storing it permanently may be the only realistic route to near-zero emissions. Carbon storage is also a necessary component of so-called negative emission technologies, such as capturing carbon dioxide from biomass combustion or directly from the air.

But where exactly can the gas be stored? Geologists identify three main options. The first is depleted oil and gas fields, which have already demonstrated their ability to hold fluids for millions of years and which are well characterised thanks to decades of production data. The second is deep saline aquifers: porous rock formations, usually more than eight hundred metres below the surface, filled with salty water unsuitable for drinking or irrigation. At that depth, the pressure is high enough for carbon dioxide to behave as a dense, supercritical fluid, which allows large quantities to be stored in a limited volume. The third, still largely experimental, involves injecting carbon dioxide into basaltic rocks, where it reacts with minerals and turns into solid carbonate within a few years.

In each case, the key requirement is a suitable seal: an impermeable layer of rock, such as clay or salt, lying above the reservoir and preventing the gas from migrating upwards. Over time, several additional trapping mechanisms come into play. Part of the carbon dioxide becomes trapped in the tiny pores of the rock, part dissolves in the formation water, and part gradually reacts to form minerals. As a result, the security of storage tends to increase rather than decrease over the centuries.

Experience suggests that the technology works. Off the coast of Norway, carbon dioxide separated from natural gas has been injected into a saline formation beneath the seabed since the mid-1990s, at a rate of around one million tonnes a year, and extensive monitoring has detected no leakage to the surface. Newer projects in the North Sea are designed to receive carbon dioxide transported by ship or pipeline from industrial plants in several European countries, creating, for the first time, a cross-border market for storage services.

The European Union has given this sector a decisive push. The directive on geological storage, adopted in 2009, already established a detailed framework covering site selection, permitting, monitoring and the eventual transfer of responsibility to the State after closure. More recently, the Net-Zero Industry Act set the target of an annual injection capacity of fifty million tonnes by 2030 and required oil and gas producers to contribute to it in proportion to their past production. The rising price of emission allowances under the Emissions Trading System also improves the business case, since emissions that are captured and stored permanently do not require allowances.

Nevertheless, significant challenges remain. Capture is costly and energy-intensive, particularly when the carbon dioxide is diluted in flue gases. Transport infrastructure, whether pipelines, port terminals or ships, must be built almost from scratch, and the investments are only justified if emitters and storage operators can rely on each other. Public perception is another concern: onshore storage projects have faced strong local opposition in several countries, which explains why most current developments are offshore. Finally, critics warn that carbon storage must not become an excuse to delay emission reductions that are achievable through efficiency, electrification or renewable energy.

For countries such as Spain, with a large cement industry but limited experience of hydrocarbon production, the question is particularly relevant. Preliminary studies have identified sedimentary formations with theoretical storage potential, but considerable work is still needed to confirm their capacity and integrity through seismic surveys and exploratory drilling. Whether this potential is realised will depend on geological knowledge, on regulatory clarity and, not least, on the confidence of the communities living above the rocks.

keyPoints: Capturing CO2 and returning it underground, long discussed, is moving beyond research and pioneering projects.

Needed for hard-to-abate process emissions (about two thirds of cement CO2 comes from limestone calcination; also lime, chemicals, waste incineration) and for negative-emission technologies (bioenergy with CCS, direct air capture).
Storage options: depleted oil and gas fields; deep saline aquifers (below about 800 m, CO2 in supercritical state); basalt mineralisation (experimental).
A sealing caprock (clay or salt) is essential; residual, dissolution and mineral trapping make storage more secure over time.
Experience: Norwegian offshore project injecting about 1 Mt a year since the mid-1990s without detected leakage; new North Sea projects create a cross-border storage market.

EU framework: 2009 CCS Directive (site selection, permits, monitoring, transfer of liability); Net-Zero Industry Act target of 50 Mt annual injection capacity by 2030 with contributions from oil and gas producers; ETS prices improve the business case.
Challenges: costly, energy-intensive capture; transport infrastructure must be built and depends on mutual reliance; onshore opposition; risk of delaying other emission reductions.
Spain: large cement sector, little hydrocarbon experience; theoretical potential needs confirmation by seismic surveys and drilling, plus regulatory clarity and public trust.

spanish.title: El Gobierno impulsa el almacenamiento subterráneo de hidrógeno renovable
spanish.text:
El Ministerio para la Transición Ecológica y el Reto Demográfico ha presentado la hoja de ruta para el desarrollo del almacenamiento subterráneo de hidrógeno renovable en España, un documento que identifica las necesidades de almacenamiento del sistema energético en el horizonte de 2040 y propone las medidas normativas, técnicas y económicas necesarias para atenderlas.

El hidrógeno renovable está llamado a desempeñar un papel fundamental en la descarbonización de aquellos sectores en los que la electrificación directa resulta difícil o costosa, como la siderurgia, la fabricación de fertilizantes, el refino o el transporte marítimo y pesado. Sin embargo, su producción mediante electrólisis depende de la disponibilidad de electricidad renovable, que varía en función de las condiciones meteorológicas y de la estación del año. Para garantizar un suministro estable a los consumidores industriales, será imprescindible disponer de capacidad de almacenamiento a gran escala que permita acumular el excedente producido en los periodos de mayor generación y utilizarlo cuando sea necesario.

Las formaciones geológicas constituyen la opción más adecuada para almacenar grandes volúmenes de hidrógeno a un coste razonable. La hoja de ruta analiza tres alternativas. Las cavidades salinas, excavadas mediante disolución controlada en formaciones de sal, ofrecen una elevada estanqueidad y permiten ciclos rápidos de inyección y extracción, por lo que se consideran la solución tecnológicamente más madura. Los yacimientos de hidrocarburos agotados y los acuíferos profundos presentan una capacidad potencial muy superior, pero plantean incertidumbres relacionadas con las posibles reacciones químicas y microbiológicas del hidrógeno con la roca y los fluidos presentes, así como con la pureza del gas recuperado.

España dispone de formaciones salinas de interés en varias cuencas sedimentarias, aunque su caracterización geológica es todavía incompleta. Por ello, el documento prevé un programa de investigación coordinado por el Instituto Geológico y Minero de España, que incluirá campañas de geofísica, la perforación de sondeos de investigación y la elaboración de un mapa nacional de potencial de almacenamiento, cuyos resultados serán de acceso público.

En el plano normativo, la hoja de ruta propone adaptar la legislación de hidrocarburos y de minas para establecer un régimen jurídico específico para el almacenamiento subterráneo de hidrógeno. Este régimen deberá regular el procedimiento de otorgamiento de los permisos de investigación y de las concesiones de almacenamiento, los requisitos de seguridad y de integridad de los pozos, los planes de vigilancia y control de la estanqueidad y las obligaciones de clausura y gestión posterior al cierre. Se prestará especial atención a la gestión de la salmuera generada durante la creación de las cavidades salinas, cuyo vertido deberá someterse a evaluación ambiental.

La hoja de ruta contempla asimismo la posibilidad de reconvertir parte de las infraestructuras gasistas existentes, incluidos los almacenamientos subterráneos de gas natural, siempre que los estudios técnicos demuestren su compatibilidad con el hidrógeno. Esta reutilización permitiría reducir costes y plazos, aunque exigirá analizar con detalle el comportamiento de los materiales de tuberías y pozos frente al fenómeno de fragilización.

Por último, el documento subraya la importancia de la cooperación con otros Estados miembros en el marco de los corredores europeos de hidrógeno, así como de la participación de las comunidades locales desde las primeras fases de los proyectos. El Ministerio abrirá en las próximas semanas un proceso de consulta pública para recabar las aportaciones de empresas, centros de investigación, administraciones territoriales y ciudadanos.

modelTranslation:
Government promotes underground storage of renewable hydrogen

The Ministry for the Ecological Transition and the Demographic Challenge has presented the roadmap for the development of underground storage of renewable hydrogen in Spain, a document that identifies the storage needs of the energy system up to 2040 and proposes the regulatory, technical and economic measures required to meet them.

Renewable hydrogen is set to play a fundamental role in decarbonising sectors where direct electrification is difficult or costly, such as steelmaking, fertiliser production, refining, and maritime and heavy transport. However, producing it by electrolysis depends on the availability of renewable electricity, which varies according to weather conditions and the time of year. To guarantee a stable supply to industrial consumers, it will be essential to have large-scale storage capacity that makes it possible to accumulate the surplus produced during periods of peak generation and to use it when needed.

Geological formations are the most suitable option for storing large volumes of hydrogen at a reasonable cost. The roadmap analyses three alternatives. Salt caverns, created by controlled dissolution in salt formations, offer a high degree of tightness and allow rapid injection and withdrawal cycles, so they are considered the most technologically mature solution. Depleted hydrocarbon fields and deep aquifers have a much greater potential capacity, but they raise uncertainties related to possible chemical and microbiological reactions between hydrogen and the rock and fluids present, as well as to the purity of the gas recovered.

Spain has salt formations of interest in several sedimentary basins, although their geological characterisation is still incomplete. The document therefore provides for a research programme coordinated by the Geological and Mining Institute of Spain, which will include geophysical surveys, the drilling of exploratory boreholes and the preparation of a national map of storage potential, the results of which will be publicly available.

On the regulatory side, the roadmap proposes amending hydrocarbons and mining legislation to establish a specific legal regime for underground hydrogen storage. This regime should govern the procedure for granting exploration permits and storage concessions, safety and well integrity requirements, plans for monitoring and controlling tightness, and obligations relating to closure and post-closure management. Particular attention will be paid to the management of the brine generated when salt caverns are created, the discharge of which must be subject to environmental assessment.

The roadmap also envisages the possibility of converting part of the existing gas infrastructure, including underground natural gas storage facilities, provided that technical studies demonstrate its compatibility with hydrogen. Such reuse would reduce costs and lead times, although it will require a detailed analysis of how pipe and well materials behave with regard to embrittlement.

Finally, the document stresses the importance of cooperation with other Member States within the framework of the European hydrogen corridors, and of involving local communities from the earliest stages of projects. In the coming weeks, the Ministry will launch a public consultation process to gather input from companies, research centres, regional and local authorities and citizens.
